title: What Context Engineering Is — and the App That Shows It
subtitle: The discipline of curating every token the model sees, met through an instrument that itemizes every call
topics: Context engineering: strategically curating the finite tokens available at inference — the attention budget
Context rot: performance degrades as the window grows, even far below the limit
The minimal high-signal principle: the smallest set of tokens that maximizes the outcome
MedFlow Copilot and the Token Lens: every AI call returns an itemized, layer-by-layer receipt
The correctness stamp: savings only count when the answer survives its answer key

analogy.title: The Itemized Restaurant Bill
analogy.text: Most teams run their AI like diners who never read the bill — they taste the answer, shrug at the total, and never learn that the wine service (a 4,700-token data dump) cost ten times the entrée (the 40 tokens of facts they actually needed). Context engineering starts the moment you demand an itemized bill: every line inspected, every charge asked to justify itself. MedFlow Copilot prints that bill for every single call — and it also checks whether the kitchen actually served what you ordered, because a cheap bill for the wrong dish is not a bargain.

antiPatterns: Judging a context setup by answer vibes alone — the answer looks fine while 99% of the spend is low-signal filler you never see, until the invoice or the latency graph forces the question
Celebrating a token reduction without a correctness check — the cheapest call in this course's grid is worthless on the one question where its answer failed the key
Assuming a bigger window fixes it — context rot means quality degrades as the window fills; more room to spend badly is not a strategy [ROT-LIT]

sections.title: The Definition, and Why It Exists
sections.body:
Context engineering is, in Anthropic's words, the practice of strategically curating and managing the finite set of tokens available to an LLM during inference ([ANTHROPIC-CE]). Three ideas hide inside that sentence. First, the window is a finite attention budget: every token consumes processing capacity, and attention thins as the count grows. Second, context rot is real — accuracy degrades as the window fills, even when you are nowhere near the hard limit; the failure axis is signal-to-noise, not size [ROT-LIT]. Third, the goal is a search problem: find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximizes the likelihood of the outcome you want.

Prompt engineering asks what words go in this message. Context engineering asks what gets included at all, in what order, fresh or cached, full or summarized. The first is a writing problem. The second is a budgeting problem — and budgets need bills you can read.

sections.title: Meet the Instrument: MedFlow Copilot and the Token Lens
sections.body:
This course refuses to teach budgeting in the abstract, so it ships an app. MedFlow Copilot is a prior-authorization portal: providers submit requests (like PA-1002, an MRI Lumbar Spine request for member M-2002), the system scores them against clinical criteria, and a reviewer works the manual-review queue with an AI copilot at their side.

The twist is the Token Lens. Every copilot call returns a TokenReceipt: input and output tokens, cost, cache behavior, latency — and the input itemized across five layers: system, retrieved, tool, history, and the user turn. The five lines always sum exactly to the input total; an instrument whose parts don't sum to its whole is lying, and this one is audited by tests. Next to the total sits the correctness stamp: the ten standing questions in this course carry deterministic answer keys derived from the seeded data, and every graded answer is stamped ✓ VERIFIED or ✗ FAILED. A saving that fails its key is stamped savings void — the single rule the whole course hangs on.

In the shipped replay mode (no API key needed) a naive ask of standing question Q1 bills 1,694 input tokens for an answer whose necessary facts fit in roughly 40 — the course's motivating ratio, under 1% signal. Every module from here on attacks that bill from a different angle. (Replay numbers are deterministic, labeled synthetic-pre-recording in every receipt; a live recording pass replaces them with API-measured usage — the labels tell you which you are reading.)

sections.question: Your copilot's answers look correct, so a teammate says the context setup is fine. WHY does the Token Lens still matter?
options: A. It doesn't — correct answers mean the context is optimal
B. Because cost, latency, and attention dilution are invisible in the answer text; a right answer can still be spending 99% of its budget on low-signal tokens that will eventually rot quality
C. Because token counts are needed for compliance reporting
D. Because the Lens makes answers more accurate by itself
sections.explanation: The answer text hides the spend. Q1's naive call is correct AND wasteful — 1,694 tokens for ~40 tokens of facts. Rot means that waste eventually costs accuracy too, not just money. The Lens exists to make the invisible spend visible before it becomes a quality problem.

sections.question: WHEN is a 70% token reduction NOT a win in this course?
options: A. When it required changing the model
B. When latency stayed the same
C. When the cheaper answer failed its answer key — a dropped key fact or a fabricated value voids the saving
D. When the cache hit rate fell
sections.explanation: Savings only count when the answer is right. The grid you'll meet in U02 contains exactly this case: a mode that cuts tokens by ~88% on one question while dropping a load-bearing fact — stamped FAILED, savings void.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong When You Skip This
items: The unread bill: a team ships a copilot, usage grows 40x, and the first itemization happens during the invoice postmortem — where they discover a static 2,000-token dump resent on every call
The vibes benchmark: 'it feels faster and cheaper' — with no receipt and no answer key, nobody can say whether quality was traded away
The trust-the-total fallacy: reading only the input total and never the layers, so nobody notices that 90% of it is one bloated layer a single lever would fix

takeaway: Context engineering begins when you itemize the bill for every AI call — and refuse to call any saving a win until the answer survives its answer key.
labUnderstand: Run MedFlow Copilot in replay mode, ask your first standing question, and audit the receipt by hand: verify the five layers sum to the total, find the dominant layer, and compute the course's motivating facts-to-input ratio (under 1%).
labBuild: Have Claude write audit_receipts.py — a script that calls the copilot API across modes and questions, checks the layers-sum-to-total reconciliation rule on every receipt, and proves itself with a --tamper flag that must produce DRIFT on every line.
